The empirical section covers several strong recent multimodal and text retrievers, includes tuned rank/score-fusion baselines, reports both NDCG@5 and Recall@5, and studies latency, storage, reranking comparisons, candidate-pool variants, role swapping, and loss variants.
Results on ViDoRe 2 show consistent improvements over the primary retrievers, including useful gains for Colnomic and Jina vision models and smaller gains for Llama-Nemo.

The efficiency analysis is valuable: the paper makes a plausible case that smaller multimodal retrievers plus lightweight text guidance can approach or exceed larger multimodal models at much lower latency and storage.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is a fairly direct adaptation of test-time query-representation optimization / pseudo-relevance feedback, with the main twist being use of a complementary retriever in a multimodal hybrid setting.

The central advantage over strong tuned score-fusion baselines is small: on ViDoRe 2, GQR averages 62.3 NDCG@5 versus 62.1 for tuned min-max score aggregation. Without significance testing or variance over splits, it is hard to know whether the representation-level optimization materially improves over simpler fusion.

The Pareto-frontier and efficiency claims are incomplete because latency/storage comparisons are shown mainly for base retrievers and GQR, not for tuned score-fusion baselines that achieve nearly the same quality and should be cheaper than iterative gradient refinement.

The evaluation is still narrow: ViDoRe 1 is saturated and gives almost no gain, while ViDoRe 2 is the only benchmark with meaningful improvements. There is limited evidence for robustness across larger corpora, different retrieval distributions, or production-like ANN/indexing settings.

The method requires an in-domain development set for tuning learning rate and iteration count, so the claimed architecture-agnostic practicality is less compelling in zero-shot or domain-shifted deployments.

Some technical details are underspecified for reproducibility, especially whether gradients flow through the consensus distribution that contains the current primary distribution, exact split/randomness details, and uniform accounting of the auxiliary text index and preprocessing costs.

The paper would benefit from stronger analysis of failure cases and from comparisons to more standard hybrid retrieval components such as sparse lexical/OCR-based retrievers, since the motivation is partly hybrid search.
